sentences.text: Eoabelisaurus was a bipedal carnivore estimated to be between 5.8 and 6.5 meters long.
Its body mass is estimated to have ranged from 730 to 800 kilograms.
The holotype specimen suffered damage where parts of the skull and the front vertebrae were eroded away before scientists could study them.
A recovered piece of the upper jaw reveals that the plates between the teeth were fused together but lacked the rough ridges seen in some relatives.
The back of the skull was tall, possessing a round eye socket and a large opening on the side similar to other ceratosaurians.
Unlike some predators, the top of the skull was not thickened and lacked any decorative bony structures.
The forelimb was very short, keeping four fingers with shortened bones in the palm.
Argentine paleontologist Diego Pol found the skeleton of this theropod near the village of Cerro Cóndor in Chubut Province in 2009.
The species Eoabelisaurus mefi was officially named and described in 2012 by Pol and his German colleague Oliver Rauhut.
The genus name combines the Greek word 'eos', meaning dawn, with Abelisaurus to highlight its status as an early relative.
The species name honors the MEF, the Paleontological Egidio Feruglio Museum in Trelew, where Pol works.
The holotype specimen MPEF PV 3990 was found in the Cañadón Asfalto Formation, a lake deposit dating from the Aalenian to Bajocian, about 170 million years ago.
The specimen consists of an almost complete skeleton with a skull from an adult or subadult individual.
Eoabelisaurus represents an unknown stage in abelisaurid evolution, possessing only some cranial modifications and a unique combination of forelimb features.
Research suggests the modification of abelisaurid forelimbs occurred in a modular fashion, starting with distal elements like fingers before affecting proximal elements.
These reduced limb proportions demonstrate that Eoabelisaurus was indeed a primitive abelisaurid.
The original describers assigned Eoabelisaurus to the basalmost position in the family Abelisauridae.
In 2018, Rafael Delcourt placed Eoabelisaurus at the base of Ceratosauridae, though he noted the classification was problematic.
This would make it the oldest known abelisaurid for forty million years.
Eoabelisaurus lived during the Lower Jurassic in the Cañadón Asfalto Basin of Argentina.
Eoabelisaurus mefi lived approximately 170 million years ago during the Bajocian stage of the Middle Jurassic in what is now South America.
The discovery of Eoabelisaurus extended the temporal range of the clade by more than 40 million years into the Middle Jurassic.
It is debated whether the placement of Eoabelisaurus at the base of Ceratosauridae is well-supported.
Descriptors noted that in cladistic analysis, a difference of a single trait could result in a more basal position within the Abelisauroidea group.
